story.title: Ajji's River
paragraphs_en: The holidays were to begin in two days. Shruthi kept instructing her brother every hour. “Anand anna, remember to pack your own spade, last time you kept borrowing mine!” Or, “Should we carry some caps…remember how your nose bled last summer?” Shruthi was a born worry-bird. She worried about the traffic; the boy in her class whom everyone else bullied or the flush in the school bathroom that refused to work. But at the moment, all she could think of was...
...Ajji's river. That gentle, wide river that flowed past her grandmother’s house near Gonikoppa, in South Kodagu. Every holiday had been spent by that river.

Swimming in it. Paddling in it. Floating paper boats and dried leaf-rafts in it. Nearly every lunch and tea-snack had been a picnic, eaten balanced comfortably on the low branches overhanging the river. The bus journey to Gonikoppa, started out peacefully. Shruthi and Anand Anna played, ‘I spy’. But soon the arguments began.

Shruthi was irritated that Anand anna had actually invited one of his friends to Ajji’s house, for a few days. “But why? How could you do that….that’s OUR river… and your silly friend, Vijay is so obsessed with his mobile phone games, our river is just wasted on him.” Anand got angry with what he thought of as Shruthi’s bossiness. She needed to know who was older. “It’s not OUR river, by the way… it belongs to every one, OK,” he said, trying to sound grown-up.

But Shruthi carried on; “ Vijay’ll spoil things for us too. He’ll only want to play in the house and Ajji will say, ‘Remember children, he is our guest….’ Oh, you never think ahead, Anand anna….” At Ajji’s house a few miles out of Gonikoppa town, the kids ran in with their back-packs even before their sprightly grandmother could come out.

Ajji gasped at how tall Shruthi had grown. And she was thrilled to find Anand no longer needed to wear glasses. “Remember the time you left your glasses by the river and the cow-herds picked it up for you on their way home?” The minute she’d uttered those words, Ajji’s expression changed. She covered her mouth with her hand, and looked worriedly at her grandchildren’s faces. Shruthi hadn’t noticed but Anand asked sharply, “What happened Ajji?”

But just then Mama entered the room with her heavy bag and Ajji rushed to embrace her daughter. Normally, immediately after arriving at Ajji’s house, after a snack , the children changed into ‘river-clothes’ and ran off under the supervision of whichever adult was available. This time Ajji insisted she’d go with them.

“But you can’t walk down that steep slope, Amma,” Mama, objected. “I’ll take them later.” But Ajji insisted she wanted to be with the kids. As Shruthi and Anand ran on ahead, whooping with excitement, Ajji tried keeping up with them. Just as they reached the last bend before the river, she called out to them.“Wait for me! I need a hand.” She didn’t want the kids to be alone, at that last turn...

Hand in hand, the three turned the corner. Shruthi, who had been literally skipping all the way, stopped, stunned. Anand froze in shock. Right up ahead of them where their beloved river ought to have been, was nothing. No water…not a drop! No chirping birds…no gurgling sounds….only a dry, silent river bed. Shruthi burst into tears. Ajji had been dreading this, which is why she’d wanted to be with the kids when they faced the shock. She hugged both her grandchildren tightly. “But where did our river go, Ajji?” Anand asked baffled.

“Come let’s sit in the shade on that rock,” Ajji said, leading the kids towards their favourite spot. But Shruthi was sobbing. “No! NO!” she shouted. “I don’t want to come here till our river comes back!”. As they walked back home, heart-broken, Ajji explained how the monsoons had failed for two years in a row. With no rains, many rivers were now dry. Earlier, only fields close to the river used the river water to irrigate their fields. But now, farmers far away from the river too, set up pumps and laid pipes to draw water to their fields. “But it is OUR river, they can’t take OUR water!” interrupted Shruthi.

Ajji patiently explained that a river belonged to every body. And that everyone needed to learn to share their river's water instead of only using it up for themselves. Initially, Shruthi had wanted to go right back to Bangalore. She was so upset. But gradually Ajji led her back to the river bed, showing her new things to look out for. She spotted crabs that had dug holes into the dry river bed, looking for moisture.

Initially she’d thought there were no birds left. Then she noticed that the white egrets were around still, waiting for the crabs to come out of their holes. Then they’d swoop down and grab a bite. With no water, Ajji was now able to show Anand and Shruthi where the kingfisher birds built their nests in holes on the steep banks… Each day, brought new discoveries.

Then came more good news - Anand’s friend, Video-game Vijay had cancelled his trip. When Anand had told him that the river had run dry, Vijay had sneered over the phone, “I had a feeling that you’d been just showing off… there WAS no river to start with, right?!” Anand was furious. But Shruthi was immensely relieved. A river that vanished was bad enough – she couldn’t have handled irritating Vijay, on top of that.

There were just a few days left of their holiday. Anand had learnt to draw water from the well. With the river dry, the local villagers came to Ajji’s well for their drinking water. Anand felt very important, helping them and like to show off the calluses he’d got on his palms, from gripping the rough rope.

Exhausted that night, the children went to sleep early. So sound was their sleep, that neither of them woke up when the first heavy drops of rain splashed noisily against their window! At first, it seemed like a small passing shower. But the rain got heavier and heavier.

And the downpour lasted for hours. Ajji came into their room, half-tempted to wake them up, to watch the rain. But decided to let them sleep. In the morning, her grandchildren could discover the miracle of their river springing back to life!

1. Did you know that there are Riparian Laws that deal with how river water is shared between those states/countries that are upstream (close to the source of the river) and those downstream. 2. Water is so precious, sometimes riots break out when there is a shortage, like between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu .

3. India and Bangladesh have a long-standing dispute on the water sharing of the Brahmaputra river, while India and Pakistan quarrel over Indus river water. 4. The same river often has different names in different countries. In Tibet, where the Brahmaputra starts, the river is called Tsangpo.

items.text_en: The holidays were to begin in two days.
Shruthi kept instructing her brother every hour.
“Anand anna, remember to pack your own spade, last time you kept borrowing mine!” Or, “Should we carry some caps…remember how your nose bled last summer?” Shruthi was a born worry-bird.
She worried about the traffic; the boy in her class whom everyone else bullied or the flush in the school bathroom that refused to work.
But at the moment, all she could think of was...
...Ajji's river. That gentle, wide river that flowed past her grandmother’s house near Gonikoppa, in South Kodagu.
Every holiday had been spent by that river.
Swimming in it.
Paddling in it.
Floating paper boats and dried leaf-rafts in it.
Nearly every lunch and tea-snack had been a picnic, eaten balanced comfortably on the low branches overhanging the river.
The bus journey to Gonikoppa, started out peacefully.
Shruthi and Anand Anna played, ‘I spy’.
But soon the arguments began.
Shruthi was irritated that Anand anna had actually invited one of his friends to Ajji’s house, for a few days.

“But why? How could you do that….that’s OUR river… and your silly friend, Vijay is so obsessed with his mobile phone games, our river is just wasted on him.” Anand got angry with what he thought of as Shruthi’s bossiness.
She needed to know who was older.
“It’s not OUR river, by the way… it belongs to every one, OK,” he said, trying to sound grown-up.
But Shruthi carried on; “ Vijay’ll spoil things for us too.

He’ll only want to play in the house and Ajji will say, ‘Remember children, he is our guest….’ Oh, you never think ahead, Anand anna….” At Ajji’s house a few miles out of Gonikoppa town, the kids ran in with their back-packs even before their sprightly grandmother could come out.
Ajji gasped at how tall Shruthi had grown.
And she was thrilled to find Anand no longer needed to wear glasses.
“Remember the time you left your glasses by the river and the cow-herds picked it up for you on their way home?” The minute she’d uttered those words, Ajji’s expression changed.
She covered her mouth with her hand, and looked worriedly at her grandchildren’s faces.
Shruthi hadn’t noticed but Anand asked sharply, “What happened Ajji?”
But just then Mama entered the room with her heavy bag and Ajji rushed to embrace her daughter.
Normally, immediately after arriving at Ajji’s house, after a snack , the children changed into ‘river-clothes’ and ran off under the supervision of whichever adult was available.
This time Ajji insisted she’d go with them.
“But you can’t walk down that steep slope, Amma,” Mama, objected.
“I’ll take them later.” But Ajji insisted she wanted to be with the kids.
As Shruthi and Anand ran on ahead, whooping with excitement, Ajji tried keeping up with them.
Just as they reached the last bend before the river, she called out to them.“Wait for me!
I need a hand.” She didn’t want the kids to be alone, at that last turn...
Hand in hand, the three turned the corner.
Shruthi, who had been literally skipping all the way, stopped, stunned.
Anand froze in shock.
Right up ahead of them where their beloved river ought to have been, was nothing.
No water…not a drop!
No chirping birds…no gurgling sounds….only a dry, silent river bed.
Shruthi burst into tears.
Ajji had been dreading this, which is why she’d wanted to be with the kids when they faced the shock.
She hugged both her grandchildren tightly.
“But where did our river go, Ajji?” Anand asked baffled.
“Come let’s sit in the shade on that rock,” Ajji said, leading the kids towards their favourite spot.
But Shruthi was sobbing.
“No! NO!” she shouted.
“I don’t want to come here till our river comes back!”.
As they walked back home, heart-broken, Ajji explained how the monsoons had failed for two years in a row.
With no rains, many rivers were now dry.
Earlier, only fields close to the river used the river water to irrigate their fields.
But now, farmers far away from the river too, set up pumps and laid pipes to draw water to their fields.
“But it is OUR river, they can’t take OUR water!” interrupted Shruthi.
Ajji patiently explained that a river belonged to every body.
And that everyone needed to learn to share their river's water instead of only using it up for themselves.
Initially, Shruthi had wanted to go right back to Bangalore.
She was so upset.
But gradually Ajji led her back to the river bed, showing her new things to look out for.
She spotted crabs that had dug holes into the dry river bed, looking for moisture.
Initially she’d thought there were no birds left.
Then she noticed that the white egrets were around still, waiting for the crabs to come out of their holes.
Then they’d swoop down and grab a bite.
With no water, Ajji was now able to show Anand and Shruthi where the kingfisher birds built their nests in holes on the steep banks… Each day, brought new discoveries.
Then came more good news - Anand’s friend, Video-game Vijay had cancelled his trip.
When Anand had told him that the river had run dry, Vijay had sneered over the phone, “I had a feeling that you’d been just showing off… there WAS no river to start with, right?!” Anand was furious.
But Shruthi was immensely relieved.
A river that vanished was bad enough – she couldn’t have handled irritating Vijay, on top of that.
There were just a few days left of their holiday.
Anand had learnt to draw water from the well.
With the river dry, the local villagers came to Ajji’s well for their drinking water.
Anand felt very important, helping them and like to show off the calluses he’d got on his palms, from gripping the rough rope.
Exhausted that night, the children went to sleep early.
So sound was their sleep, that neither of them woke up when the first heavy drops of rain splashed noisily against their window!
At first, it seemed like a small passing shower.
But the rain got heavier and heavier.
And the downpour lasted for hours.
Ajji came into their room, half-tempted to wake them up, to watch the rain.
But decided to let them sleep.
In the morning, her grandchildren could discover the miracle of their river springing back to life!
1. Did you know that there are Riparian Laws that deal with how river water is shared between those states/countries that are upstream (close to the source of the river) and those downstream.
2. Water is so precious, sometimes riots break out when there is a shortage, like between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu .
3. India and Bangladesh have a long-standing dispute on the water sharing of the Brahmaputra river, while India and Pakistan quarrel over Indus river water.
4. The same river often has different names in different countries.
In Tibet, where the Brahmaputra starts, the river is called Tsangpo.
